troponin.title: Cardiac Troponin (cTnI / cTnT)
troponin.definition: Regulatory proteins of the myocardial contractile apparatus released into circulation upon cardiomyocyte necrosis. High-sensitivity assays (hs-cTn) are the gold-standard biomarker for diagnosing acute myocardial infarction.
troponin.pearl: Rises within 2–3 hours (hs-cTn), peaks at 24–48 hours, and remains elevated for 7–10 days.

stemi.title: ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)
stemi.definition: Acute coronary syndrome caused by complete, transmural coronary artery occlusion resulting in myocardial necrosis and characteristic ST-segment elevations (or new LBBB/STEMI equivalents) on 12-lead ECG.
stemi.pearl: Time is myocardium: immediate reperfusion (PCI ≤ 90 min) is mandatory without waiting for troponin results.

nstemi.title: Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI)
nstemi.definition: Acute myocardial infarction characterized by elevated cardiac troponin levels without persistent ST-segment elevation, typically resulting from partial or transient coronary occlusion causing subendocardial necrosis.
nstemi.pearl: Fibrinolytics are contraindicated in NSTEMI—manage with DAPT, anticoagulation, and risk-stratified PCI.

ua.title: Unstable Angina (UA)
ua.definition: Myocardial ischemia at rest, of new onset (< 2 months), or accelerating in frequency/severity (crescendo) WITHOUT detectable cardiomyocyte necrosis (normal serial troponins).
ua.pearl: Distinguished from NSTEMI solely by negative serial cardiac troponins.

pci.title: Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI)
pci.definition: Catheter-based mechanical revascularization (balloon angioplasty and drug-eluting stent placement) used to restore coronary blood flow in ACS.
pci.pearl: Preferred over fibrinolysis for STEMI when First Medical Contact-to-device time is ≤ 90 min (or ≤ 120 min with transfer).

dapt.title: Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT)
dapt.definition: Combined administration of low-dose aspirin (COX-1 inhibitor) plus a P2Y12 receptor inhibitor (ticagrelor, prasugrel, or clopidogrel) to prevent stent thrombosis and recurrent ischemic events.
dapt.pearl: Ticagrelor or prasugrel is generally preferred over clopidogrel in ACS patients undergoing PCI (avoid prasugrel if prior stroke/TIA).

wellens.title: Wellens Syndrome
wellens.definition: Biphasic (Type A) or deeply symmetric inverted T waves (Type B) in leads V2–V3 observed during a pain-free interval, indicating critical proximal LAD stenosis.
wellens.pearl: Stress testing is strictly contraindicated—patients require urgent coronary angiography due to imminent risk of massive anterior STEMI.

dewinter.title: de Winter T-Wave Pattern
dewinter.definition: Upsloping ST-segment depression (> 1 mm) at the J-point in precordial leads V1–V6 continuing into tall, prominent, symmetric T waves, often with ST elevation in aVR.
dewinter.pearl: A high-risk STEMI equivalent indicating acute proximal LAD occlusion—treat with emergent PCI.

prinzmetal.title: Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) Angina
prinzmetal.definition: Transient, focal coronary artery vasospasm causing rest angina (typically midnight to early morning) accompanied by transient ST-segment elevations that resolve with vasodilators.
prinzmetal.pearl: Strongly associated with smoking; treat with calcium channel blockers and nitrates, and avoid non-selective beta-blockers.

killip.title: Killip Classification
killip.definition: Bedside physical exam classification stratifying acute MI severity: Class I (no HF), Class II (rales/S3/JVD), Class III (acute pulmonary edema), Class IV (cardiogenic shock).
killip.pearl: Higher Killip class correlates linearly with 30-day mortality.

ckmb.title: Creatine Kinase-MB (CK-MB)
ckmb.definition: Cardiac-enriched isoenzyme of creatine kinase that rises 4–6 hours after myocardial injury, peaks at 24 hours, and normalizes within 48–72 hours.
ckmb.pearl: Because troponin remains elevated for up to 10 days, CK-MB is useful for detecting acute reinfarction occurring days after an index MI.

dressler.title: Dressler Syndrome
dressler.definition: Delayed immune-mediated (autoimmune) pericarditis occurring 2–10 weeks post-MI due to myocardial neoantigen exposure, presenting with pleuritic pain, fever, and friction rub.
dressler.pearl: Treat with high-dose aspirin + colchicine; avoid systemic glucocorticoids initially unless refractory (impairs myocardial scar healing).

grace.title: GRACE Risk Score
grace.definition: Validated scoring model predicting in-hospital and 6-month mortality in ACS using age, HR, SBP, creatinine, Killip class, cardiac arrest, ST deviation, and elevated biomarkers.
grace.pearl: GRACE score > 140 mandates an early invasive strategy (< 24 hours) in NSTEMI/UA.

fondaparinux.title: Fondaparinux
fondaparinux.definition: Indirect synthetic Factor Xa inhibitor (pentasaccharide) used for anticoagulation in NSTEMI/UA, particularly when an ischemia-guided (conservative) approach is chosen.
fondaparinux.pearl: Do NOT use as sole anticoagulant during PCI due to risk of catheter thrombosis—supplement with UFH if proceeding to PCI.

scad.title: Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection (SCAD)
scad.definition: Non-atherosclerotic, non-traumatic separation of the coronary arterial wall creating an intramural hematoma that compresses the true lumen.
scad.pearl: Classic board presentation: young/middle-aged woman without traditional cardiovascular risk factors (associated with fibromuscular dysplasia & pregnancy).

curb65.title: CURB-65 Score
curb65.definition: Clinical prediction rule for community-acquired pneumonia severity: Confusion, Urea (BUN > 19 mg/dL), Respiratory rate ≥ 30/min, BP < 90/60 mmHg, Age ≥ 65 years.
curb65.pearl: Score 0–1: outpatient; 2: consider inpatient/short stay; ≥ 3: inpatient + assess for ICU.

macrolide.title: Macrolide Antibiotics
macrolide.definition: Bacteriostatic protein synthesis inhibitors (50S ribosomal subunit) including azithromycin and clarithromycin with potent coverage against atypical respiratory pathogens.
macrolide.pearl: Monitor for QTc prolongation and torsades de pointes; rising S. pneumoniae macrolide resistance limits monotherapy in areas with > 25% resistance.

procalcitonin.title: Procalcitonin
procalcitonin.definition: Peptide precursor of calcitonin upregulated in response to bacterial endotoxins and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α), suppressed by interferon-γ in viral infections.
procalcitonin.pearl: Used to guide antibiotic de-escalation/discontinuation rather than withholding initial empiric therapy in suspected CAP.

gdmt.title: Guideline-Directed Medical Therapy (GDMT)
gdmt.definition: Four foundational mortality-reducing drug classes in HFrEF: ARNI (or ACEi/ARB), evidence-based beta-blocker, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA), and SGLT2 inhibitor.
gdmt.pearl: Initiate all four pillars early at low doses and titrate upward as tolerated.

aniongap.title: Serum Anion Gap
aniongap.definition: Calculated as Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻), normally 8–12 mEq/L, representing unmeasured serum anions (primarily albumin, plus ketoacids or lactate in metabolic acidosis).
aniongap.pearl: In DKA, insulin therapy continues until the anion gap closes (< 12 mEq/L)—not merely until blood glucose normalizes.

acs.title: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)
acs.summary: **Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)** encompasses a clinical spectrum of acute myocardial ischemia resulting from sudden reduction in coronary blood flow—most commonly due to atherosclerotic plaque disruption and superimposed thrombosis. It comprises [[hl:{{term:ua|Unstable Angina (UA)}}]], [[hl:{{term:nstemi|NSTEMI}}]], and [[hl:{{term:stemi|STEMI}}]].

items.text: **ACS Spectrum**: Driven by acute coronary plaque rupture/erosion leading to thrombus formation and myocardial ischemia.

children.text: **NSTE-ACS** (Non-ST-Elevation ACS): Includes {{term:ua|Unstable Angina}} and {{term:nstemi|NSTEMI}}; typically caused by [[hl:partial or intermittent coronary occlusion]] producing subendocardial ischemia.
**Unstable Angina (UA)**: Clinical ischemia with [[hl:normal serial cardiac troponins]] (no cardiomyocyte necrosis).
**NSTEMI**: Clinical ischemia with [[hl:elevated cardiac troponins]] (> 99th percentile URL) indicating myocardial necrosis.
**STEMI**: Caused by [[hl:complete, persistent coronary occlusion]] resulting in transmural myocardial injury/necrosis with persistent ST-segment elevation.

items.text: **Universal Classification of MI (4th Universal Definition)**: Categorizes myocardial infarction into 5 mechanistic subtypes.

children.text: **Type 1 MI**: Spontaneous MI due to atherosclerotic plaque rupture, ulceration, or dissection with intraluminal thrombus.
**Type 2 MI**: Secondary to [[hl:ischemic oxygen supply–demand mismatch]] without acute atherothrombosis (e.g., severe anemia, sepsis, tachyarrhythmia, hypertensive crisis).
**Type 3 MI**: Cardiac death with symptoms suggestive of ischemia before biomarkers could be obtained.
**Type 4 / Type 5 MI**: Procedure-related MI associated with {{term:pci|PCI}} (Type 4a/b/c) or CABG (Type 5).

blocks.title: Clinical Pearl: Distinguishing UA vs. NSTEMI
blocks.text: At initial presentation, UA and NSTEMI are clinically indistinguishable because both present with ischemic chest pain and non-diagnostic or ST-depression/T-wave inversion ECG changes. Only [[hl:serial {{term:troponin|troponin}} measurements]] (at 0h and 1–3h) differentiate NSTEMI (elevated) from UA (normal).

blocks.caption: Comparison of Acute Coronary Syndrome Subtypes
rows: [[hl:Elevated]] (do NOT delay PCI waiting for result)
Normal, ST depression, or T-wave inversion
ST depression, T-wave inversion, or normal
[[hl:Persistent ST elevation]] in ≥ 2 contiguous leads or new LBBB
Indicated if PCI delay > 120 min (door-to-needle ≤ 30 min)

items.text: **Atherosclerotic Plaque Disruption (~90% of Type 1 ACS)**:

children.text: **Plaque rupture**: Thin fibrous cap ruptures, exposing thrombogenic lipid core and tissue factor.
Vulnerable plaques typically feature a large necrotic lipid core, macrophage infiltration, matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) degradation, and a fibrous cap < 65 µm.
**Plaque erosion**: Endothelial denudation over a proteoglycan-rich plaque (increasingly recognized in women and younger smokers).

items.text: **Non-Atherosclerotic Causes of ACS**:

children.text: **{{term:prinzmetal|Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) Angina}}**: Focal epicardial coronary vasospasm causing transient ST elevations, often in smokers or triggered by cocaine/triptans.

**{{term:scad|Spontaneous Coronary Artery Dissection (SCAD)}}**: Intramural hematoma compressing the true lumen; classic in [[hl:young/peripartum women without traditional CAD risk factors]] (associated with fibromuscular dysplasia).
**Coronary Embolism & Arteritis**: Infective endocarditis vegetations, paradoxical emboli, atrial myxoma, Kawasaki disease, or Takayasu arteritis.

items.text: **Major Cardiovascular Risk Factors**:

children.text: **Modifiable**: Hypertension, hyperlipidemia (elevated LDL-C), [[hl:diabetes mellitus]] (considered a CAD risk equivalent), smoking, obesity, sedentary lifestyle.
**Non-Modifiable**: Advanced age (men ≥ 45 yrs, women ≥ 55 yrs), male sex, premature family history (1st-degree male relative < 55 yrs or female < 65 yrs).

items.text: **Thrombotic Cascade**: Plaque rupture exposes subendothelial collagen and von Willebrand factor → platelet adhesion (GpIb) and activation → conformational change in [[hl:GpIIb/IIIa receptors]] → fibrinogen cross-linking and fibrin clot stabilization.
**Ischemic Progression (Wavefront Phenomenon)**:

children.text: Necrosis begins in the [[hl:subendocardium]] (highest wall tension and oxygen demand, furthest from epicardial vessels) within 20–30 minutes of complete occlusion.
Progresses outward toward the epicardium over 3–6 hours until becoming transmural unless collateral flow or reperfusion intervenes.

items.text: **Adaptive & Post-Ischemic Myocardial States**:

children.text: **Myocardial stunning**: Reversible contractile dysfunction persisting for hours to days after brief ischemia despite restoration of normal blood flow.
**Hibernating myocardium**: Chronic downregulation of contractile function in response to chronic hypoperfusion that recovers after revascularization.

items.text: **Typical Anginal Chest Pain**:

children.text: **Quality & Location**: Substernal squeezing, heaviness, or pressure (**Levine sign**: clenched fist over sternum) lasting [[hl:> 20 minutes]] and unrelieved by rest or sublingual nitroglycerin.
**Radiation**: Left arm/shoulder, neck, jaw, epigastrium, or interscapular region.
**Autonomic Symptoms**: Diaphoresis (strongest positive predictor), nausea/vomiting, dyspnea, presyncope.

items.text: **Atypical Presentations ("Anginal Equivalents")**:

children.text: Isolated unexplained dyspnea, epigastric discomfort, fatigue, syncope, or acute confusion without chest pain.
Most common in [[hl:older adults, women, and patients with diabetes mellitus]] (autonomic neuropathy blunts visceral pain sensation).

items.text: **Physical Examination Findings**:

children.text: **Auscultation**: [[hl:S4 gallop]] (stiff, non-compliant ischemic ventricle), S3 gallop (systolic dysfunction/HF), or new holosystolic murmur at apex (papillary muscle dysfunction → mitral regurgitation).
**{{term:killip|Killip Classification}}**: Assesses acute heart failure severity (Class I: clear lungs → Class IV: cardiogenic shock with SBP < 90 mmHg and pulmonary edema).
**Vascular Signs**: Bilateral radial pulse/BP discrepancies (> 20 mmHg) should immediately prompt evaluation for acute aortic dissection.

blocks.title: Red Flag: Silent / Atypical MI in Diabetics
blocks.text: Never rule out ACS based solely on absence of chest pain in elderly or diabetic patients. Acute unexplained dyspnea, diaphoresis, or new-onset pulmonary edema warrants an immediate 12-lead ECG.
Rapid diagnostic triage centers on immediate 12-lead ECG interpretation combined with serial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin assays and targeted bedside evaluation.

items.text: **Door-to-ECG Time**: Obtain and interpret a 12-lead ECG within [[hl:10 minutes]] of emergency department arrival.
**STEMI ECG Diagnostic Criteria** (new ST elevation at the J-point in ≥ 2 anatomically contiguous leads):

children.text: **Limb & lateral/other chest leads**: ≥ 1 mm (0.1 mV) in all leads except V2–V3.
**Leads V2–V3 (sex/age-specific thresholds)**: [[hl:≥ 2.0 mm in men ≥ 40 yrs]], ≥ 2.5 mm in men < 40 yrs, and [[hl:≥ 1.5 mm in women]].
Repeat ECGs every 15–30 minutes if initial tracing is non-diagnostic but clinical suspicion remains high.

items.text: **Anatomical ECG Territories**:

children.text: **Anterior / Anteroseptal (LAD)**: V1–V4 (highest risk for LV systolic failure & cardiogenic shock).
**Inferior (RCA ~80%, LCx ~20%)**: [[hl:II, III, aVF]] → always obtain [[hl:right-sided lead V4R]] to evaluate for right ventricular MI.
**Lateral (LCx / Diagonal LAD)**: I, aVL, V5–V6.
**Posterior (LCx / RCA)**: [[hl:ST depression + tall R waves in V1–V3]] → confirm with posterior leads **V7–V9** showing ST elevation ≥ 0.5 mm.

items.text: **Critical STEMI Equivalents (Treat as Emergent Occlusion)**:

children.text: **{{term:wellens|Wellens Syndrome}}**: Deeply inverted or biphasic T waves in V2–V3 when pain-free (proximal LAD stenosis) → [[hl:avoid stress testing]].
**{{term:dewinter|de Winter T Waves}}**: Upsloping ST depression at J-point in V1–V6 with tall symmetric T waves.

**Modified Sgarbossa Criteria** (in pre-existing LBBB or ventricular paced rhythm): Concordant ST elevation ≥ 1 mm, concordant ST depression ≥ 1 mm in V1–V3, or discordant ST elevation ≥ 25% of preceding S wave depth.

items.text: **{{term:troponin|High-Sensitivity Cardiac Troponin (hs-cTn)}}**: Preferred biomarker of myocardial injury.

children.text: Rises within [[hl:2–3 hours]], peaks at 24–48 hours, and remains elevated for [[hl:7–10 days]].
Non-ACS causes of troponin elevation include myocarditis, PE, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy, sepsis, renal failure (reduced clearance), and hypertensive emergency.

items.text: **{{term:ckmb|CK-MB}}**: Normalizes within 48–72 hours; useful primarily for detecting [[hl:acute reinfarction]] occurring several days after an index MI.
**Portable Chest X-Ray**: Rule out pneumothorax, pneumonia, pulmonary edema, and [[hl:widened mediastinum (aortic dissection)]] before giving antithrombotics.
**Bedside Transthoracic Echocardiography (TTE)**: Identifies regional wall motion abnormalities, LVEF, pericardial effusion, and mechanical complications.
**Baseline Labs**: CBC (check hemoglobin/platelets before anticoagulation), BMP (renal function & K⁺/Mg²⁺ to prevent arrhythmias), lipid panel, and coagulation profile.

blocks.title: High-Yield Exam Tip: Revisit the Classic 'MONA' Mnemonic
blocks.text: Modern guidelines no longer support routine **O**xygen or **M**orphine for all ACS patients. Only administer oxygen if [[hl:SpO₂ < 90%]] (hyperoxia causes coronary vasoconstriction), and reserve morphine for refractory pain because it delays oral P2Y12 absorption.

items.text: **Antiplatelet Therapy (Immediate)**:

children.text: **Aspirin**: [[hl:162–325 mg non-enteric coated, chewed]] immediately in all patients without true anaphylaxis.
**P2Y12 Inhibitor ({{term:dapt|DAPT}})**: Add loading dose of [[hl:ticagrelor]] (180 mg), prasugrel (60 mg, only after coronary anatomy known & no prior stroke/TIA), or clopidogrel (300–600 mg).

items.text: **Anticoagulation**: Initiate [[hl:unfractionated heparin (UFH)]] or low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin); {{term:fondaparinux|fondaparinux}} is preferred in ischemia-guided NSTEMI with high bleeding risk (never sole agent during PCI).
**Anti-Ischemic & Hemodynamic Therapy**:

children.text: **Nitrates (Sublingual/IV Nitroglycerin)**: Relieves ischemic pain via preload reduction and coronary vasodilation; [[hl:contraindicated if SBP < 90 mmHg, PDE-5 inhibitor use within 24–48h, or RV infarction]].

**Oral Beta-Blocker** (e.g., metoprolol): Initiate within 24 hours if hemodynamically stable to reduce myocardial oxygen demand; avoid in acute decompensated HF, bradycardia, heart block, or cocaine-induced ACS.
**High-Intensity Statin**: Atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg initiated immediately for plaque stabilization regardless of baseline LDL.

items.text: **STEMI (Emergent Reperfusion — Target Ischemic Time < 12 Hours)**:

children.text: **Primary {{term:pci|PCI}} (Preferred)**: First medical contact (FMC)-to-device time [[hl:≤ 90 minutes]] at PCI-capable center (or ≤ 120 min if transfer required).
**Fibrinolysis (Alteplase / Tenecteplase)**: Indicated ONLY if PCI cannot be achieved within 120 minutes; target door-to-needle time [[hl:≤ 30 minutes]].

**Absolute Contraindications**: [[hl:Prior intracranial hemorrhage (anytime)]], ischemic stroke within 3 months, active internal bleeding, suspected aortic dissection, CNS neoplasm/AVM, or severe head trauma within 3 months.

items.text: **NSTE-ACS (NSTEMI / UA) — Risk-Stratified Invasive Approach**:

children.text: **Immediate Invasive (< 2 hours)**: Refractory angina, hemodynamic instability/cardiogenic shock, life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias, or acute mechanical complications.
**Early Invasive (< 24 hours)**: Elevated troponin, dynamic ST/T changes, or [[hl:{{term:grace|GRACE score}} > 140]].
**Fibrinolytics**: Strictly [[hl:contraindicated in NSTEMI/UA]] (no benefit and increased hemorrhagic risk).

blocks.title: Red Flag: Right Ventricular (RV) Infarction
blocks.text: Suspect RV infarction in any patient with an inferior STEMI presenting with the triad of [[hl:hypotension, elevated JVP (Kussmaul sign), and clear lung fields]] (+ ST elevation in V4R). Management requires [[hl:IV normal saline boluses]] to maintain RV preload; **strictly avoid nitrates and diuretics**, which precipitate severe shock.

items.text: **Cocaine-Induced ACS**: Treat acutely with [[hl:IV benzodiazepines]] (reduces sympathetic outflow) + aspirin + nitrates; use phentolamine or calcium channel blockers for refractory hypertension/vasospasm; [[hl:avoid non-selective beta-blockers]] acutely (risk of unopposed α-adrenergic coronary vasoconstriction).
**{{term:prinzmetal|Vasospastic Angina}}**: First-line therapy is [[hl:calcium channel blockers]] (amlodipine/diltiazem) + long-acting nitrates + smoking cessation.
**{{term:dapt|DAPT}}**: Aspirin 81 mg daily indefinitely + P2Y12 inhibitor for at least [[hl:12 months]] post-ACS (shorter duration only if high bleeding risk).
**Neurohormonal Blockade**:

children.text: **ACE Inhibitor (or ARB)**: Initiate within 24 hours for anterior MI, LVEF ≤ 40%, hypertension, or diabetes to prevent adverse LV remodeling.
**MRA (Eplerenone / Spironolactone)**: Add for patients already on ACEi + beta-blocker with [[hl:LVEF ≤ 40%]] and symptomatic HF or diabetes (monitor K⁺ and Cr).

items.text: **Lifestyle & Vaccination**: Structured cardiac rehabilitation, complete smoking cessation, and annual influenza vaccination (reduces recurrent CV events).
**Arrhythmias (Most Common Cause of Early Death)**:

children.text: [[hl:Ventricular fibrillation (VF)]]: Leading cause of pre-hospital and first-24h mortality post-MI; manage with immediate unsynchronized defibrillation.

**Conduction Blocks**: Inferior MI (RCA → AV nodal artery) causes transient sinus bradycardia/Mobitz I (responds to atropine); anterior MI causes infranodal Mobitz II/complete heart block (requires temporary pacing).

items.text: **Mechanical Complications (Typically 3–7 Days Post-MI due to Macrophage Weakening)**:

children.text: **[[hl:Papillary Muscle Rupture]]**: Often posteromedial papillary muscle (single blood supply from PDA in inferior MI) → acute severe mitral regurgitation, flash pulmonary edema, new holosystolic murmur.
**Interventricular Septal Rupture**: Holosystolic murmur at left lower sternal border + [[hl:O₂ step-up from right atrium to right ventricle]] on Swan-Ganz catheterization.
**Left Ventricular Free Wall Rupture**: Sudden hemodynamic collapse, [[hl:cardiac tamponade, and pulseless electrical activity (PEA)]] (highest mortality).

items.text: **Pericardial & Mural Complications**:

children.text: **Early Fibrinous Pericarditis (1–3 days)**: Pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward + friction rub; treat with aspirin (avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen/indomethacin due to impaired scar healing).
**{{term:dressler|Dressler Syndrome}} (2–10 weeks)**: Autoimmune pericarditis + fever + elevated ESR; treat with [[hl:high-dose aspirin + colchicine]].

**True LV Aneurysm (> 2 weeks)**: Outpouching of thinned scarred wall (often anterior) showing [[hl:persistent ST elevation weeks after MI]] + risk of mural thrombus (treat with anticoagulation if thrombus present).

cap.title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP)
cap.summary: **Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP)** is an acute infection of the pulmonary parenchyma acquired outside the hospital (or < 48 hours after admission). Management relies on severity stratification ({{term:curb65|CURB-65}} / PSI) and targeted empiric antibiotic therapy.

items.text: **Typical Bacterial Pathogens**:

children.text: **Streptococcus pneumoniae**: [[hl:Overall most common bacterial cause of CAP]]; rusty sputum, lobar consolidation, lancet-shaped gram-positive diplococci.
**Haemophilus influenzae**: Common in [[hl:COPD and active smokers]]; pleomorphic gram-negative coccobacilli.
**Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA/MSSA)**: Classic [[hl:post-influenza pneumonia]] causing severe necrotizing cavitary infiltrates.
**Klebsiella pneumoniae**: Alcohol use disorder / aspiration; currant-jelly sputum and bulging interlobar fissure.

items.text: **Atypical Pathogens ("Walking Pneumonia" — No Cell Wall / Intracellular)**:

children.text: **Mycoplasma pneumoniae**: Young adults in crowded settings (dorms/military); dry cough, bilateral interstitial infiltrates, [[hl:cold agglutinins (IgM) & bullous myringitis]].
**Legionella pneumophila**: Contaminated water systems (AC cooling towers); pneumonia + [[hl:GI symptoms (watery diarrhea), hyponatremia, and relative bradycardia]].

blocks.caption: Typical vs. Atypical vs. Aspiration Pneumonia
rows: Sudden onset, high fever, rigors, productive purulent sputum
Insidious onset, low-grade fever, dry cough, extrapulmonary signs
Foul-smelling sputum in patients with dysphagia / alcohol / seizure
[[hl:Dependent lung zones]] (RLL upright; posterior RUL/RLL supine)

items.text: **Chest Radiography (Gold Standard for Confirmation)**: Required to demonstrate a new parenchymal infiltrate alongside clinical symptoms.
**Microbiologic Testing**:

children.text: **Outpatient CAP**: Routine sputum/blood cultures are [[hl:NOT recommended]] (treat empirically).
**Severe Inpatient / ICU CAP**: Obtain blood cultures, sputum Gram stain/culture, and [[hl:Legionella & pneumococcal urinary antigen tests]].
**{{term:procalcitonin|Procalcitonin}}**: Helps guide antibiotic discontinuation once clinically stable, not initial withholding.

blocks.title: Clinical Pearl: Elderly / Volume-Depleted CXR
blocks.text: Severely dehydrated or neutropenic patients may initially have a falsely normal chest radiograph that develops a visible infiltrate only after IV fluid resuscitation.

items.text: **Disposition via {{term:curb65|CURB-65 Score}}**: Score 0–1 → outpatient; Score 2 → inpatient admission; Score ≥ 3 → inpatient/evaluate for ICU.
**Outpatient Empiric Regimens**:

children.text: **Healthy (no comorbidities, no recent abx)**: [[hl:Amoxicillin 1 g TID]] (preferred) or doxycycline (or {{term:macrolide|macrolide}} ONLY if local pneumococcal resistance < 25%).

**With Comorbidities** (chronic heart/lung/liver/renal disease, DM, alcoholism): [[hl:Amoxicillin-clavulanate (or cephalosporin) + macrolide/doxycycline]], OR respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin/moxifloxacin) monotherapy.

items.text: **Inpatient Non-ICU Regimens**: [[hl:IV β-lactam (ceftriaxone) + macrolide (azithromycin)]] OR respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy.

**ICU / Severe CAP**: IV β-lactam + either macrolide or respiratory fluoroquinolone; add [[hl:vancomycin or linezolid]] if prior MRSA, or antipseudomonal β-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam / cefepime) if *Pseudomonas* risk factors.

blocks.title: Red Flag: Empyema & Parapneumonic Effusion
blocks.text: Persistent fever or leukocytosis after 48–72 hours of appropriate antibiotics warrants repeat imaging to evaluate for parapneumonic effusion/empyema. Perform diagnostic thoracentesis; [[hl:pH < 7.20, glucose < 60 mg/dL, or frank pus]] mandates urgent tube thoracostomy drainage.

hf.title: Heart Failure (HFrEF & HFpEF)
hf.summary: **Heart Failure (HF)** is a complex clinical syndrome resulting from structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or ejection of blood, categorized primarily into **HFrEF** (LVEF ≤ 40%) and **HFpEF** (LVEF ≥ 50%).

items.text: **LVEF Categories**: [[hl:HFrEF (LVEF ≤ 40%)]], HFmrEF (41–49%), and [[hl:HFpEF (LVEF ≥ 50%)]].
**Left- vs. Right-Sided Congestion**:

children.text: **Left HF**: Dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND), bibasilar crackles, [[hl:S3 gallop]] (volume overload).
**Right HF**: Elevated JVP, hepatojugular reflux, hepatomegaly, ascites, bilateral pitting edema (most commonly caused by left-sided HF).

items.text: **Four Pillars of Mortality-Reducing {{term:gdmt|GDMT}} in HFrEF**:

children.text: **ARNI (Sacubitril/Valsartan)** (preferred over ACEi/ARB; wait [[hl:36-hour washout]] when switching from ACEi to avoid angioedema).
**Evidence-Based Beta-Blocker**: [[hl:Carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, or bisoprolol]] (initiate only when euvolemic/compensated).
**MRA**: Spironolactone or eplerenone (if NYHA II–IV, eGFR > 30, K⁺ < 5.0).
**SGLT2 Inhibitor**: [[hl:Dapagliflozin or empagliflozin]] (reduces mortality & hospitalizations in BOTH HFrEF and HFpEF regardless of diabetes status).

items.text: **Loop Diuretics (Furosemide / Torsemide)**: Essential for symptom relief of congestion, though they do not independently reduce mortality.

blocks.title: Red Flag: Drugs to Avoid in HFrEF
blocks.text: Avoid [[hl:non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers]] (verapamil, diltiazem), NSAIDs, and thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone), as they worsen fluid retention and precipitate decompensation.

dka.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
dka.summary: **Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)** is a life-threatening acute metabolic complication of severe insulin deficiency and counter-regulatory hormone excess characterized by the triad of **hyperglycemia**, **ketonemia**, and **high-{{term:aniongap|anion gap}} metabolic acidosis**.

items.text: **Diagnostic Triad**: Glucose > 250 mg/dL (note: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause [[hl:euglycemic DKA]] with glucose < 250 mg/dL), arterial pH < 7.30 / HCO₃⁻ < 18 mEq/L, and positive serum/urine ketones (β-hydroxybutyrate predominant).
**Clinical Features**: Polyuria/polydipsia, abdominal pain/vomiting, [[hl:Kussmaul respirations]] (deep, rapid compensatory hyperventilation), fruity acetone breath, severe volume depletion.
**Step 1 — Aggressive IV Fluids**: Begin with [[hl:0.9% normal saline]] (1–1.5 L in first hour) before insulin to restore perfusion and lower counter-regulatory hormones.
**Step 2 — Check Potassium BEFORE Starting Insulin**:

children.text: K⁺ < 3.3 mEq/L: [[hl:HOLD insulin]] and aggressively replete K⁺ first (insulin drives K⁺ intracellularly → fatal arrhythmias).
K⁺ 3.3–5.2 mEq/L: Start IV regular insulin AND add 20–30 mEq KCl per liter of IV fluid.

items.text: **Step 3 — Close the Anion Gap**: Add [[hl:D5W (dextrose)]] when serum glucose falls below 200–250 mg/dL while continuing IV insulin until the [[hl:{{term:aniongap|anion gap}} closes (< 12 mEq/L)]].

blocks.title: Clinical Pearl: Subcutaneous Transition Overlap
blocks.text: Once the anion gap normalizes and the patient can tolerate oral intake, administer subcutaneous long-acting insulin and overlap with the IV insulin infusion for [[hl:1–2 hours]] before stopping the drip to prevent rebound ketoacidosis.

acs.stem: A 66-year-old man with hypertension and hyperlipidemia is brought to the emergency department 45 minutes after developing severe crushing substernal chest pain radiating to his left shoulder, accompanied by diaphoresis and nausea. Vital signs are temperature 36.8°C, pulse 54/min, respirations 20/min, blood pressure 82/50 mmHg, and SpO₂ 96% on room air. Physical examination reveals jugular venous distension that increases on inspiration and clear lung fields bilaterally. A 12-lead ECG shows 3-mm ST-segment elevations in leads II, III, and aVF, with ST depression in aVL. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate pharmacologic intervention alongside aspirin and heparin?

options.text: Sublingual nitroglycerin
IV normal saline bolus
IV metoprolol
IV furosemide
IV alteplase prior to obtaining chest X-ray

acs.explanation: This patient presents with an **inferior STEMI (leads II, III, aVF)** complicated by **right ventricular (RV) infarction**, evidenced by the classic triad of **hypotension, elevated JVP (with Kussmaul sign), and clear lung fields**. The ischemic right ventricle is acutely preload-dependent; therefore, immediate **IV normal saline fluid resuscitation** is required alongside emergent PCI. **Nitrates (A)** and **diuretics (D)** abruptly reduce preload and can precipitate fatal cardiogenic shock. **Beta-blockers (C)** worsen bradycardia and hypotension. **Alteplase (E)** is only considered if primary PCI is delayed > 120 min and contraindications (like aortic dissection) are excluded.

acs.stem: A 58-year-old man presents after experiencing two 15-minute episodes of severe substernal pressure at rest earlier this morning. He is currently completely pain-free. His vital signs are BP 136/82 mmHg, HR 72/min, SpO₂ 98%. A 12-lead ECG obtained while pain-free reveals deeply symmetric, inverted T waves in leads V2 and V3 without pathologic Q waves. Initial high-sensitivity troponin is mildly elevated. Which of the following is the next best step in management?

options.text: Exercise treadmill stress test prior to discharge
Dobutamine stress echocardiography
Urgent coronary angiography with PCI readiness
Outpatient Holter monitoring and statin initiation
Immediate IV tenecteplase

acs.explanation: Deeply inverted (or biphasic) T waves in V2–V3 during a pain-free interval represent **Wellens syndrome**, which is highly specific for critical stenosis of the **proximal left anterior descending (LAD)** coronary artery. Patients require **urgent coronary angiography** for revascularization. **Stress testing (A, B)** is strictly contraindicated because inducing myocardial oxygen demand can precipitate a massive, fatal anterior STEMI. **Tenecteplase (E)** is contraindicated in NSTE-ACS without ST elevation.

acs.stem: A 71-year-old woman who underwent medical management for an inferoposterior STEMI 5 days ago suddenly develops acute dyspnea and profound hypotension (BP 76/48 mmHg). Cardiac auscultation reveals a new, harsh grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur best heard at the cardiac apex radiating to the axilla, along with diffuse bilateral pulmonary crackles. Which of the following mechanical complications is most likely responsible?

options.text: Left ventricular free wall rupture
Posteromedial papillary muscle rupture
Dressler autoimmune pericarditis
Interventricular septal rupture
Left ventricular apical aneurysm

acs.explanation: Acute severe mitral regurgitation (new apical holosystolic murmur radiating to the axilla) and flash pulmonary edema 3–7 days after an inferior MI is classic for **posteromedial papillary muscle rupture**. The posteromedial papillary muscle is especially vulnerable because it has a single blood supply from the posterior descending artery (PDA), whereas the anterolateral muscle has dual supply (LAD + LCx). **Ventricular septal rupture (D)** causes a harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border with an O₂ step-up in the RV. **Free wall rupture (A)** causes cardiac tamponade and PEA without a murmur.

cap.stem: A 68-year-old man with a history of well-controlled hypertension presents with 3 days of fever, productive cough, and pleuritic chest pain. Vitals: T 38.9°C, BP 104/68 mmHg, HR 102/min, RR 32/min, SpO₂ 91% on room air. He is alert and oriented to person, place, and time. Labs show BUN 24 mg/dL and WBC 15,800/mm³. Chest X-ray demonstrates a right lower lobe consolidation. Based on his CURB-65 score, what is the most appropriate disposition and empiric antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Outpatient discharge with oral amoxicillin
Outpatient discharge with oral azithromycin
Inpatient admission with IV ceftriaxone plus azithromycin
Inpatient admission with IV vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam
Immediate ICU admission with oral doxycycline

cap.explanation: Calculating **CURB-65**: Confusion (0), Urea/BUN > 19 mg/dL (+1: BUN is 24), RR ≥ 30/min (+1: RR is 32), BP < 90/60 (0), Age ≥ 65 (+1: age 68). Total **CURB-65 = 3**, indicating severe CAP requiring **inpatient admission** (and evaluation for ICU level of care). Standard empiric inpatient non-ICU therapy is an **IV β-lactam (ceftriaxone) plus a macrolide (azithromycin)** or respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy. Broad MRSA/Pseudomonas coverage (D) is reserved for ICU severity with specific risk factors.

hf.stem: A 62-year-old woman with HFrEF (LVEF 30%) currently taking lisinopril, carvedilol, and furosemide is seen in clinic with NYHA Class II dyspnea. Vital signs show BP 122/74 mmHg, HR 66/min, Cr 1.1 mg/dL, K⁺ 4.3 mEq/L. Her cardiologist decides to switch lisinopril to sacubitril/valsartan. Which instruction is critical during this transition?

options.text: Discontinue carvedilol 24 hours prior
Observe a 36-hour washout period after stopping lisinopril
Overlap lisinopril and sacubitril/valsartan for 3 days
Stop furosemide indefinitely before starting ARNI

hf.explanation: Switching from an ACE inhibitor (lisinopril) to an ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) requires a mandatory **36-hour washout period** because dual inhibition of ACE and neprilysin markedly elevates bradykinin levels and precipitates life-threatening **angioedema**.

dka.stem: A 22-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is admitted with DKA (glucose 520 mg/dL, pH 7.16, anion gap 26 mEq/L, initial K⁺ 3.0 mEq/L). After initiating a 1 L bolus of 0.9% normal saline, what is the next most appropriate step?

options.text: Begin IV regular insulin bolus and drip immediately
Administer IV sodium bicarbonate to raise pH > 7.25
Hold insulin and administer IV potassium chloride first
Switch IV fluids immediately to D5W

dka.explanation: In DKA, total body potassium is severely depleted despite often normal/high initial serum levels. Because this patient is already hypokalemic (**K⁺ < 3.3 mEq/L**), starting insulin immediately would drive potassium intracellularly and trigger fatal ventricular arrhythmias. **Hold insulin and replete IV potassium first** until K⁺ ≥ 3.3 mEq/L.
